name: Čertovy hlavy (Devil's Heads)
label: Čertovy hlavy
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/537028676: the OpenStreetMap point 'Čertovy hlavy'.
notes: Giant faces carved into a sandstone rock face, the best-known sight of the village.

text.description: Čertovy hlavy, or the Devil's Heads, are a pair of huge faces carved straight into the sandstone at Želízy. Each sculpture stands about 9 metres high. They were made by the sculptor Václav Levý between 1841 and 1846, and they are a one-off in the Czech Republic for sheer size. They are also described as the second largest carved heads in the world, behind only Mount Rushmore. Time and weather have worn the stone, which gives the faces a rough, ancient look that suits a photograph. In 2011 the private owner had the pine forest around them cleared, so the heads can now be seen openly, including from the I/9 road. Close by there are two more sandstone reliefs, known as Harfenice (the Harpist) and Had (the Snake), which make good extra frames if you have time. Because the heads are so tall and you stand so close, the main challenge is fitting them in. Then move in for a tighter shot of the carved features. Look out for the texture of the weathered stone, which shows best when the light is not flat. Keep your phone level so the rock does not seem to lean.
text.geographic_location: The heads are in the municipality of Želízy in the Central Bohemian Region. The surrounding pine forest was cut down in 2011, so they can be seen from the I/9 road.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot. From there the heads are 11 m to the east, just a few steps away. The phone icon on the map is about 10 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x), because the heads are about 9 m high and you are only around 11 m away. Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural look, and the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details of the carved faces.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 10 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. You are looking straight at the rock sculptures, so turn to face east and keep the phone upright.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and place the heads on one of the vertical lines so they fill the frame. Take one wide shot with some rock and trees around for scale, then a tighter shot of the faces. Try a low angle with the ultra-wide to emphasise their height. If you walk a little way around the site, the nearby Harfenice (Harpist) and Had (Snake) reliefs make good extra photos.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stone to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the carved detail does not wash out. Skip portrait mode, as the subject is a large rock face and not a person.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: You face east, so afternoon sun will be behind you; check how the light falls on the carved faces when you arrive. Thin cloud can also help, as it softens harsh shadows on the stone.

text.access_note: The heads stand on privately owned land, so check the official site before you go for current access arrangements.

name: Klácelka
label: Klácelka
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Blaník' (4 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/1485046368: the OpenStreetMap point 'Klácelka'.
notes: Rock formation and viewpoint in the forest south of the village.

text.description:
Klácelka is a man-made cave cut into sandstone in the forest near Želízy. It is a sculpture as much as a cave. The young sculptor Václav Levý carved it in the 1840s, and it is named after František Klácel, a theologian and philosopher. Levý turned the rock into an imagined Blaník, the hall where legendary heroes sleep. Around the entrance and inside you can find the Hussite leaders Jan Žižka and Prokop Holý, the sleeping army, and dwarf figures forging weapons for them. Reliefs inside the cave illustrate a fable by Klácel.

It photographs well because the carved figures sit right beside the opening, so one frame can hold the cave mouth, the faces and the rock wall. The forecourt below the rock face is the natural place to shoot it straight on. The light in the forest is usually soft and uneven, so tap on the carvings to set focus and brightness, and take a few frames with slightly different exposure. The cave is on the blue-marked trail, so you can combine it with a walk to other Levý works nearby. The cave is in a protected heritage area, so keep to the paths, don't touch the carvings, and photograph respectfully.
text.geographic_location: Klácelka lies in the forest just outside Želízy, on the blue-marked tourist trail that loops through the area. It sits in a sandstone rock face, with an open forecourt in front of the cave.
text.directions_text: Start from the centre of Želízy and head south on the blue-marked trail; the cave is roughly a kilometre away. Follow the blue markers on foot until you reach the rock face and the open space in front of the cave. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the cave mouth and the carved figures together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are pressed against the opposite edge of the forecourt and can't fit the whole rock face in. Use telephoto (2x or more) for close-ups of the faces and reliefs.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the photo shows the cave entrance framed by the carved figures of Jan Žižka and Prokop Holý, with the sleeping army and the dwarves forging weapons in the rock around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Face the rock squarely so the entrance sits in the middle and the carved figures on either side balance each other. Switch on gridlines to keep the vertical edges of the rock straight. Then step closer for a second shot of a single face or relief using 2x or higher.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the carved figures to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky or bright forest gaps wash out the rock. If it is dark inside the cave, use night mode and hold the phone steady against a wall or your other arm.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Overcast days or the soft light of morning and late afternoon usually suit the sandstone best. Midday sun through the trees can cast patchy shadows across the carvings.

text.access_note: The cave is freely reachable on foot along the blue tourist trail from Želízy, and it lies in a protected heritage area, so check the official site before you go for any local rules.

text.description: Želízy is a quiet village in the Kokořínsko countryside, and its best-known sight sits in the pine forest above it: the Čertovy hlavy, or Devil's Heads. They are two huge faces carved into the sandstone by the sculptor Václav Levý in the first half of the 19th century. Each is roughly 9 m tall, and they are the largest work in a wider set of rock carvings around the village. That scale is what makes them fun to photograph. The heads fill the frame, the pines close in around them, and you can get a sense of the Liběchovka valley dropping away below. The sandstone is weathered, so the faces look soft and ancient rather than crisp, which works well in photos. The forest in front was cleared in 2011, so the heads can now also be spotted from the I/9 road, but the walk up gives you far better angles. If you have time, the Harfenice cave nearby, with its faded relief of a woman with a harp, makes a good second stop. Take a few frames from further back to show the heads against the trees, then step closer for the faces. Please don't climb on the carvings. They are fragile, and climbing is already causing damage.
text.geographic_location: The Čertovy hlavy are in the pine forest on the sandstone just south of the centre of Želízy, a village in Mělník District, Central Bohemian Region. They sit above the village and the Liběchovka valley.
text.directions_text: No railway station or tram stop is close by. The I/9 road runs through Želízy, so that is the route to the village. From the village, follow the blue trail up into the pine forest. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit a head, the rock and the trees into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. If your phone has telephoto (2x-5x), use it for the faces and carved details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (the two heads in the pine forest above Želízy, reached by the blue trail from the village). The two roughly 9 m sandstone heads carved by Václav Levý, framed by the forest and the Liběchovka valley below.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place a head off-centre, leaving some forest around it to show its size. Take one wide shot with the valley behind, then a closer one of a face. If you want a different view of the carvings, try the Harfenice cave nearby.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stone to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if bright sky shows through the trees. Dappled light under the pines can look harsh, so check the screen before you move on.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Even, soft light such as an overcast day or a calm morning should suit the weathered stone. Bright, patchy sun through the trees can make the faces hard to read.

text.access_note: The heads are freely accessible in the forest above the village, but the stone is fragile, so please don't climb on it. Check the official site before you go for any local restrictions.
